blocks.text: We can represent the strength of a magnetic field B by lines of force in the same way as for an electric field. Then the population of these lines per unit area passing through a surface perpendicular to the field represents the magnetic flux.

blocks.title: Magnetic flux
blocks.text: The magnetic flux through a patch of area A is the number of magnetic lines passing through this area. If B represents the number of lines passing through unit area placed perpendicular to the field, then B = phi/A ... (10.4).

The surface A may not be perpendicular to the field; that is, the normal to the surface may make an angle theta with B (Fig. 10.5). Then we use the component of B (B cos theta) along the vector area A (Fig. 10.6). Therefore the flux passing through the surface is phi_B = BA cos theta ... (10.5). As B and A are both vectors, we can write phi_B = B.A ... (10.6). Equation 10.6 shows that phi_B is a scalar quantity: the magnetic flux phi_B through a plane element of area A in a uniform magnetic field B is given by the dot product of B and A.

blocks.alt: Horizontal magenta field lines labelled B run to the right through a tilted yellow plane area. A green vector A rises from the area, normal to it, at angle theta above the field direction (dashed reference line).
blocks.caption: Figure 10.5: A plane area A whose normal makes an angle theta with B (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.5).

blocks.alt: Vector B points horizontally to the right; vector A rises from the same point at angle theta. A dashed line drops from the tip of B perpendicular to A; the part of A up to that point is labelled B cos theta.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.6: The component B cos theta of B along the vector area A (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.6).

blocks.text: A is a vector whose magnitude is the area of the element and whose direction is along the normal to the surface of the element, and theta is the angle between the directions of B and A (Fig. 10.5). In Fig. 10.7(a) the field is directed along the normal to the area, so theta is zero (cos 0 = 1) and the flux is maximum, equal to BA. When the field is parallel to the plane of the area (Fig. 10.7b), the angle between the field and the normal is 90 degrees (cos 90 = 0), so the flux through the area in this orientation is zero. For a curved surface in a uniform field, the surface is divided into a number of small elements, each assumed plane, and the flux through the whole surface is the sum of the contributions of all the elements using Eq. 10.5.

blocks.alt: (a) A yellow area stands across horizontal field lines B, with the green vector A along the field. (b) A yellow area lies flat along the field lines B, with A pointing straight up, at 90 degrees to B.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.7: (a) Field along the normal to the area: maximum flux; (b) field parallel to the area: zero flux (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.7).

blocks.title: Weber and flux density
blocks.text: From the definition of the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux is N m A^-1, which is called the weber (Wb). According to Eq. 10.5 the magnetic induction B is the flux per unit area of a surface perpendicular to B; hence it is also called the magnetic flux density, with unit Wb m^-2. Therefore the magnetic field strength is measured in Wb m^-2 or N A^-1 m^-1 (tesla).

blocks.title: Example 10.2
blocks.text: A rectangular loop of wire, 25 cm long and 20 cm wide, is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 1.2 T. Determine the magnetic flux through the loop for the three orientations shown in Fig. 10.8, where the loop makes 30, 45 and 60 degrees with the field. Solution: A = 20 cm x 25 cm = 5 x 10^-2 m^2. (a) The angle between B and the area vector A is theta = 60 degrees: phi_B = BA cos theta = 1.2 T x 5 x 10^-2 m^2 x 0.5 = 3 x 10^-2 Wb. (b) theta = 45 degrees: phi_B = 1.2 x 5 x 10^-2 x 0.707 = 4.2 x 10^-2 Wb. (c) theta = 30 degrees: phi_B = 1.2 x 5 x 10^-2 x 0.866 = 5.2 x 10^-2 Wb.

blocks.alt: Three panels (a), (b), (c), each with vertical magenta field lines pointing down and a flat rectangular loop seen edge-on as a yellow strip, tilted at 30, 45 and 60 degrees from the vertical field direction.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.8: A rectangular loop at three orientations in a uniform magnetic field (Example 10.2) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.8).

blocks.alt: For each of the three orientations: the loop edge, vector B pointing straight down and the area vector A normal to the loop. The loop makes 30, 45 and 60 degrees with B, and the angle between B and A is 60, 45 and 30 degrees.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.9: Angles between B, the loop and the area vector A for the three orientations (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.9).
